Do not attribute the gait disorder to knee osteoarthritis or diabetic neuropathy
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH needs an insidious gait disturbance after age 40 lasting at least 3 to 6 months with cognitive or urinary symptoms, no antecedent cause, ventriculomegaly (Evans index greater than 0.3) not explained by atrophy, and a CSF opening pressure of 5 to 18 mmHg (7 to 24.5 cmH2O) [Relkin_2005].
DESH and an acute callosal angle support the diagnosis; here Evans 0.40, DESH and a callosal angle of 70 degrees [Nakajima_2021].

The tap test removes 30 to 50 mL and repeats the timed gait measures at 2 to 4 and 24 hours [Nakajima_2021]; a 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off. Its sensitivity is 26% to 61% and its PPV 73% to 100%, so a single negative tap does not exclude shunt-responsive iNPH [Marmarou_2005].
Knee osteoarthritis gives a painful antalgic gait and diabetic neuropathy a sensory ataxia; neither produces short shuffling steps with start freezing that improve after CSF removal.

patient.history_present_illness: A 78-year-old retired schoolteacher with type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait difficulty. Her daughter arranged the admission after noticing her mother's steady functional decline over the past two years. The patient initially attributed her walking difficulties to her knee arthritis, but her orthopedic surgeon noted that her gait pattern was atypical for osteoarthritis, with short shuffling steps without significant knee pain during ambulation. She describes her feet as feeling 'stuck to the ground' when she tries to initiate walking. She has fallen four times in the past year, all without loss of consciousness. She now uses a rollator walker for all ambulation. Cognitive changes include increasing difficulty with finances (she accidentally paid the same bill three times in one month), and her daughter reports she repeats questions and has difficulty following complex television programs. She has been managing this independently but admits that she now struggles to follow her daughter's instructions for smartphone use. Urinary incontinence has been present for approximately 18 months; she wears protective pads daily and has stopped attending her church book club due to embarrassment. A head CT obtained six months ago by her primary care physician was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. She was referred by her primary care physician for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary incontinence.
